title: Meeting Teresa (1567)
hook: he joins her reform of the Carmelites: barefoot, poor, prayerful

segments.voice: Yesterday, a poor childhood: hunger, a hospital, and a safe future turned down. Your line was he knew poverty first. Did you do the small thing for someone unwell? Today, the young friar meets the woman who'll change his life. Day two hundred fifty-six.

Medina del Campo, 1567. John is twenty-five, newly ordained, and restless. He's a Carmelite, but he wants more silence and more prayer than his house gives him. He's quietly decided to leave and join the Carthusians, the strictest, most silent monks he knows. Then someone tells a visiting nun about him. She's fifty-two, famous, and in town to open a new convent. She asks to meet him. They talk. And by the end of the conversation, he isn't going anywhere. Today's word is what she talked him into.
screen: `A RESTLESS YOUNG PRIEST.` → `ABOUT TO LEAVE FOR MORE SILENCE.` → `ONE CONVERSATION WITH TERESA.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Discalced comes from the Latin for unshod, without shoes. Teresa's reformed Carmelites were called the Discalced, the barefoot ones. In practice they usually wore simple rope sandals, not bare feet on Spanish stone. But the name stuck, and it said what they were about: poverty, simplicity, a life stripped down for prayer. Second, the pitch. Teresa told John he didn't need to leave the Carmelites to find silence. He could help her bring it back to them. She was already reforming convents of nuns. Now she wanted a house of friars living the same way: poor, enclosed, praying for hours a day. He agreed, on one condition: that she not make him wait too long. Third, the farmhouse. In 1568 he moved into the first house of Discalced friars, in a tiny hamlet called Duruelo. It was a half-ruined farmhouse. The chapel was in the attic, so low you had to kneel. Teresa visited and said later it moved her deeply. That's when he took a new name, John of the Cross. Fourth, the shoes. Why shoes? Think of Moses at the burning bush. God tells him, in the Douay-Rheims: "put off the shoes from thy feet: for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Taking off shoes is an old sign: you're somewhere holy, and you're not in charge here. The Discalced wanted to live their whole life that way. Not everyone welcomed the reform, though. Tomorrow we'll see how some of John's own brothers answered it.
screen: `DISCALCED: WITHOUT SHOES.` · `DON'T LEAVE. HELP ME REFORM.` · `A FARMHOUSE IN DURUELO.` · `SHOES OFF ON HOLY GROUND.` · then, large: `PUT OFF THE SHOES FROM THY FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take off your shoes for prayer. If you're wearing shoes, slip them off, and feel the floor under your feet. If you're driving or can't, just picture it. Sit, and let your feet rest flat. Notice the ground holding you up. If you pray, you can treat this little spot as holy ground for two minutes, and simply be present to God there. If you don't, let the bare feet remind you to slow down and be where you are. The bell holds the time.
Discalced. From the Latin for unshod: Teresa and John's reformed Carmelites, living poor, simple and prayerful, often in rope sandals. Today's word.
Your line: the barefoot friars. Today, find one thing you could strip down, a routine, a closet, a calendar, and take one thing out of it. Day two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: The Discalced Carmelites, friars and nuns, still live Teresa and John's reform today, with hours of daily silent prayer, and many wear sandals as part of their habit.

original.note: Latin: unshod, from dis- (without) and calceus (shoe). the root of Discalced.

trapdoor: what you thought: monks who didn't wear shoes.
what it means: Teresa and John's reformed Carmelites, living poor and prayerful, with bare feet as the sign.
what a scholar hears: discalceatus, unshod; the first Discalced friars' house opened at Duruelo on November 28, 1568.

sources.quoted: put off the shoes from thy feet: for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground

sources.ref: Teresa of Ávila, The Book of Foundations, ch. 3, 13–14

notes: Meeting at Medina del Campo in 1567, John's intention to join the Carthusians, and his condition that she not delay: Foundations ch. 3; paraphrased. Confirm.
Teresa was born March 1515, so she was 52 in 1567; John was 25. Confirm.
Duruelo: first house of Discalced friars, November 28, 1568; the low attic chapel and Teresa's visit are in Foundations ch. 14. Confirm details.
Rope sandals (alpargatas) vs. bare feet: stated plainly; confirm.
Pronunciation given in classical Latin; church Latin would say 'dee-shal-cheh-AH-toos'. Keeper may prefer either.
